messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: unit scale! [moved from stan-users]
parts:
[moved to stan-dev]

My question is about what you want the program to look like.
That program you had didn't have any constrained parameters,
so the "raw" parameters would be the same as the unconstrained
parameters, so you wouldn't need this. If you add constrained
parameters, then you get the Jacobian. I don't know why either
you or Andrew want the unconstrained parameters.

- Bob

> On Apr 22, 2016, at 10:17 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
> This is kind of expert, yes; but a raw parameter is used all the time in about any hierarchical model which uses the Matt trick. I mean OK, you end up getting that Jacobian warning and need to know that you don't need to worry about it as the Jacobian from shift and scale is a constant, but that could be explained in the manual, no?
>
> I think it would be very useful, I am using this as a sort of hack to not being able to specify the mass matrix myself - and in fact this unit scaling and centering is better than specifying the mass matrix since this will always be only a wild guess, but Stan's adaptation is there to really find out what the mass matrix should be.
>
> Sebastian
>
> On Friday, April 22, 2016 at 4:06:24 PM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Oops --- Amtrak sent that last one.
>
> What I meant is that the code uses a raw parameter.
>
> Given people's confusions about Jacobians, we've been
> very reluctant to literally expose the unconstrained
> parameters.
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Apr 22, 2016, at 9:52 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >
> > Do you have a specific proposal? Your code
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >> On Apr 22, 2016, at 3:34 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>
> >> To clarify: NUTS runs amazingly fast when centering and scaling... as a side note... this is the huge benefit of the Matt trick which automatically unit-scales all those hierarchical parameters.
> >>
> >> BTW, I wrote my model in a way like
> >>
> >> parameters {
> >> vector[15] phi_raw;
> >> }
> >> tansformed parameters {
> >> real parameter1;
> >> ....
> >> vector[15] phi;
> >>
> >> phi <- phi_location + phi_scale .* phi_raw;
> >>
> >> parameter1 <- phi[1];
> >> }
> >> model {
> >> phi ~ mvn_normal_cholesky(prior);
> >> }
> >>
> >> The phi_location and phi_scale are my guesses for the scale and location (for most applications the same as the mvn prior, but not in my application).
> >>
> >> Wouldn't it make sense to allow this in the Stan language in a principled way? I mean, it would be great to have direct access to the unconstrained space for users.
> >>
> >> Sebastian
> >>
> >> On Friday, April 22, 2016 at 1:14:48 AM UTC+2, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> >> Yes, unit scale is great.
> >> A
> >>
> >>> On Apr 21, 2016, at 4:34 PM, Sebastian Weber
> >>>
> >>> Hi Alp,
> >>>
> >>> hmmm I can try, but I never had good experience with full rank ADVI (way too slow). Moreover, I have ~1000 patients and 15 parameters out of which 2 are patient specific, which leaves me with ~2000 parameters which are mostly glued together by a hierarchy. Is that big or small for ADVI? Or have there been updates to full rank ADVI recently?
> >>>
> >>> On another note, I have essentially solved my performance problems by centering and rescaling to unit scale; quite amazing what the effect of that is, really!
> >>>
> >>> Sebastian

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: Re: unit scale! [moved from stan-users]
parts:
Hi!

Ahh... now I get it. Not really, I did not code the constrained ones, i.e. I had some standard deviations which were coded on log-space, but then I anyway used a prior on the log-scale.

Good modeling practice is to go to unconstrained in any case. There are models where this is hard and I love in these cases the clever tricks Stan does in the background for me. So this feature is dangerous for some of those involved types, yes. I missed your discussion around this and the rationale for not doing it, sorry.

However, having done this type of programming - I don't see a big problem in letting people do this themselves. Moreover, this way I can leave the variables which are anyway at unit-scale (Matt trick) as they are and I don't mess around with them. So maybe this feature is not so badly needed...

Sebastian

Hi!

In a nutshell I am using the unconstrained space to shortcut warmup as I do know in my example the scale and location of my parameters very well beforehand. So I shift and scale from the raw parameters to the used parameters in the model. The speedups I am getting are tremendous - around factor ~3x(!).

The Stan program is quite large and I would have to remove a few details here and there, but if you need more details than the above description, I could do it.

Sebastian
